slides.title: Motivations
points: Motivation explains why an actor attacks. Security+ scenarios often give you the goal and expect you to identify the likely motivation.
Security+ Objective 2.1: compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.

slides.title: Data Exfiltration
slides.teach: Stealing or transferring data out of an environment without authorization.

course.learn: Stealing or transferring data out of an environment without authorization.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker wants to remove protected data from the organization.
Customer database theft, Source code theft, Sensitive file extraction

course.why: Stolen data can be sold, leaked, used for espionage, or used as leverage.
course.example: An attacker uploads a customer database to an external server.
course.check_q: What motivation describes unauthorized transfer of data out of an environment?

slides.title: Espionage
slides.teach: Obtaining confidential information for strategic, political, military, or competitive advantage.

course.learn: Obtaining confidential information for strategic, political, military, or competitive advantage.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker wants secret intelligence.
Government intelligence gathering, Trade-secret theft

course.why: The stolen information itself provides strategic advantage beyond immediate resale value.
course.example: A foreign actor steals defense research to gain strategic insight.
course.check_q: Which motivation focuses on gaining strategic intelligence?

slides.title: Service Disruption
slides.teach: Making a system or service unavailable or unreliable.

course.learn: Making a system or service unavailable or unreliable.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker wants the service to stop working.
DDoS, Sabotage, Operational outage

course.why: Disruption can create financial loss, reputational damage, or operational impact.
course.example: Attackers overwhelm an online service so customers cannot use it.
course.exam: Take the service down → SERVICE DISRUPTION.

slides.title: Blackmail
slides.teach: Using threatened disclosure, harm, or leverage to force a victim to comply or pay.

course.learn: Using threatened disclosure, harm, or leverage to force a victim to comply or pay.

breakdown.explanation: Do what I want or I expose/harm something.
Threat to leak stolen data, Extortion

course.why: The attacker uses the threat itself as leverage against the victim.
course.example: A group threatens to publish stolen records unless the organization pays.
course.exam: Pay or I leak it → BLACKMAIL.
course.check_q: What motivation uses threatened disclosure as leverage?

breakdown.explanation: The attacker wants profit.
Fraud, Ransomware, Credential resale, Cryptocurrency theft

course.why: Financial gain is one of the most common motivations for cybercrime.
course.example: Criminals steal payment-card data to sell it.
course.check_q: Which motivation best fits theft for resale?

slides.title: Philosophical / Political Beliefs
slides.teach: Acting to promote or defend an ideology, cause, or political position.

course.learn: Acting to promote or defend an ideology, cause, or political position.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker is motivated by a belief or cause.
Hacktivism, Protest attacks

course.why: The goal may be attention, protest, influence, or ideological pressure rather than profit.
course.example: A group attacks an organization because it opposes the organization's political position.
course.exam: Cause / ideology → PHILOSOPHICAL OR POLITICAL BELIEFS.
course.check_q: Which motivation is based on ideology or political position?

slides.title: Ethical
slides.teach: Acting for a perceived defensive, research, or public-good purpose rather than malicious personal benefit.

course.learn: Acting for a perceived defensive, research, or public-good purpose rather than malicious personal benefit.

breakdown.explanation: The goal is to improve or protect security, typically with authorization or responsible intent.
Authorized security research, Responsible vulnerability testing

course.why: Ethical motivation distinguishes defensive or public-good activity from malicious exploitation.
course.example: An authorized researcher tests a system and reports the vulnerability to the owner.
course.check_q: Which motivation best fits authorized security research intended to improve defenses?

slides.title: Revenge
slides.teach: Retaliating against a person or organization because of a grievance.

course.learn: Retaliating against a person or organization because of a grievance.

breakdown.explanation: The actor wants to get even.
Disgruntled employee sabotage, Data deletion after termination

course.why: Personal grievances can motivate destructive or unauthorized actions.
course.example: A terminated employee deletes company files to retaliate.
course.check_q: Which motivation is based on retaliation for a grievance?

slides.title: Disruption / Chaos
slides.teach: Causing disorder, confusion, damage, or instability for its own sake or as a primary objective.

course.learn: Causing disorder, confusion, damage, or instability for its own sake or as a primary objective.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker wants chaos or destruction.
Destructive malware, Random destructive attacks

course.why: The objective may be instability rather than profit, intelligence, or a specific political demand.
course.example: Destructive malware is released broadly with no demand for payment.
course.check_q: Which motivation best fits destruction without a clear financial or intelligence goal?

slides.title: War
slides.teach: Supporting military or national conflict objectives through cyber operations.

course.learn: Supporting military or national conflict objectives through cyber operations.

breakdown.explanation: Cyber activity is part of national or military conflict.
Critical infrastructure attacks, Military network targeting

course.why: Cyber operations can support strategic, military, and national objectives during conflict.
course.example: A state-backed group attacks power infrastructure during an armed conflict.
course.check_q: Which motivation is tied directly to military or national conflict?

blocks.title: Identify the goal, then name the motivation
items: Steal the files → Data Exfiltration
The immediate goal is moving protected information out of the environment.
Example: An attacker uploads a customer database to an external server.
Secret strategic intelligence → Espionage
The goal is intelligence advantage rather than simply selling the data.
Example: A foreign actor steals defense research to gain strategic insight.
Take the service down → Service Disruption
The target is availability.
Example: Attackers overwhelm an online service so customers cannot use it.
Pay or I leak it → Blackmail
The attacker uses threatened disclosure or harm as leverage.
Example: A group threatens to publish stolen records unless the victim pays.
Money → Financial Gain
The main objective is economic benefit.
Example: Criminals steal payment-card data for resale.
Cause / ideology → Philosophical or Political Beliefs
The action is driven by a political, social, or philosophical position.
Example: A hacktivist group attacks an organization it opposes.
Defensive/public-good purpose → Ethical
The intent is to improve or protect security rather than cause harm.
Example: An authorized researcher tests a system and reports the vulnerability.
Get even → Revenge
The actor retaliates because of a personal or organizational grievance.
Example: A terminated employee deletes company data.
Cause disorder → Disruption / Chaos
The attacker primarily wants instability or damage.
Example: Destructive malware is released without a clear financial objective.
National conflict → War
Cyber activity supports military or geopolitical conflict.
Example: A state-backed group attacks critical infrastructure during a conflict.
blocks.example: Memory: Steal data · Secret intelligence · Take it down · Threaten · Money · Belief · Ethical · Revenge · Chaos · War.

questions.q: An attacker uploads a company’s customer database to an external server. Which motivation is most directly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Data exfiltration is the unauthorized transfer of data out of an environment.

questions.q: A foreign actor steals defense research to gain strategic intelligence rather than sell it. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: Espionage focuses on obtaining confidential information for strategic advantage.

questions.q: Attackers overwhelm an online service so customers cannot access it. Which motivation is most direct?
questions.explanation: The goal is to make the service unavailable.

questions.q: A criminal group threatens to publish stolen medical records unless the victim pays. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: Blackmail uses threatened disclosure or harm as leverage.

questions.q: Attackers steal payment-card data and sell it to other criminals. Which motivation is most likely?
questions.explanation: The primary objective is economic benefit.

questions.q: A group defaces a website to protest the organization’s political position. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: The attack is driven by ideological or political beliefs.

questions.q: An authorized security researcher tests a system and responsibly reports the vulnerability to the owner. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: The activity is intended to improve security rather than cause harm.

questions.q: A terminated employee deletes company files because of a personal grievance. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: The actor is retaliating because of a grievance.

questions.q: Destructive malware is released broadly with no demand for payment and no apparent intelligence objective. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: The primary objective is disorder and destruction.

questions.q: A state-backed group attacks critical infrastructure during an armed conflict to support national military objectives. Which motivation best fits?
questions.explanation: The cyber activity directly supports national or military conflict.
